title: The Potential Effects of Wind Power Facilities on Resident and Migratory Birds in Eastern Wisconsin
abstract:
1. Point surveys were conducted at increasing distances (1 km, 2 km, 4 km and 8 km) from Horicon Marsh during 1996-97 in order to assess the potential impacts of wind turbine construction on diurnal birds. 
2. Numbers of individual birds were highest during spring and autumn. During these seasons, bird abundance was higher in the vicinity of the Marsh (1 km). The decrease in numbers of birds with increasing distance from the marsh was most pronounced during autumn. 
3. Numbers of species were highest near the Marsh during spring and, to a lesser extent, during summer, but no significant trend in species richness was evident during autumn, when the average species richness was lowest. 
4. During spring and autumn, significantly more birds were recorded in the western and northwestern directions from Horicon Marsh, indicating a potentially important geographic pattern of bird activity. 
5. Based on abundance and flight elevations, diurnal bird species that are most likely to be affected by wind turbine construction near Horicon Marsh include Canada Goose, Mallard, Red-tailed Hawk, American Crow, Ring-billed Gull, Turkey Vulture, Sandhill Crane and Red-winged Blackbird. 6. A separate analysis of bird activity and mortality was conducted at the site of two newly constructed wind turbines near Shirley, Wisconsin. On average, species richness at this site was greater than that at the Horicon Study area during spring, summer, and autumn. 
7. Bird abundance and species richness were lower near the wind turbines than at distances of 1 km, 2 km, and 4 km. The difference in numbers of individual birds (abundance) was not statistically significant, but the difference in numbers of species was significant during both spring and early summer. 
8. Based on abundance and flight elevations, diurnal species most likely to be affected by wind turbines at this study area include Ring-billed Gull, Rock Dove, Red-winged Blackbird, European Starling, Red-tailed Hawk, Canada Goose, American Crow, and Common Grackle. 
9. Intensive surveys for bird mortality in the vicinity of the wind turbines yielded only one bird death, which can be confidently, attributed to collision with one of the wind turbines. This bird (a Red-eyed Vireo) represents a nocturnal spring migrant. 
10. An experiment with planted bird carcasses suggests that observers using a standard survey method was able to find only about 40-50% of the small bird carcasses present in the fields near the wind turbines. Predators remove approximately 26% of the carcasses over a 10 day period. Even accounting for these factors, however, bird mortality at the two wind turbines was low during this study period.

## _**The Potential Effects of Wind Power Facilities on Resident and Migratory Birds in Eastern Wisconsin**_

**A report submitted to the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources Bureau of Integrated Science Services 1350 Femrite Drive Monona, WI  53716**

_by_

**Robert W. Howe and Ryan Atwater Richter Museum of Natural History University of Wisconsin-Green Bay**

**29 March 1999**

**Richter Museum of Natural History Special Research Report No. 5**

## Summary

1. Point surveys were conducted at increasing distances (1 km, 2 km, 4 km and 8 km) from Horicon Marsh during 1996-97 in order to assess the potential impacts of wind turbine construction on diurnal birds.

2. Numbers of individual birds were highest during spring and autumn.  During these seasons, bird abundance was higher in the vicinity of the Marsh (1 km).  The decrease in numbers of birds with increasing distance from the marsh was most pronounced during autumn.

3. Numbers of _species_ were highest near the Marsh during spring and, to a lesser extent, during summer, but no significant trend in species richness was evident during autumn, when the average species richness was lowest.

4. During spring and autumn, significantly more birds were recorded in the western and northwestern directions from Horicon Marsh, indicating a potentially important geographic pattern of bird activity.

5. Based on abundance and flight elevations, diurnal bird species that are most likely to be affected by wind turbine construction near Horicon Marsh include Canada Goose, Mallard, Red-tailed Hawk, American Crow, Ring-billed Gull, Turkey Vulture, Sandhill Crane and Red-winged Blackbird.  These birds fly at significantly higher elevations during autumn, presumably creating a greater risk of collision with wind turbines.

6. A separate analysis of bird activity and mortality was conducted at the site of two newly constructed wind turbines near Shirley, Wisconsin.  On average, species richness at this site was greater than that at the Horicon Study area during spring, summer, and autumn.

7. Bird abundance and species richness were lower near the wind turbines than at distances of 1 km, 2 km, and 4 km.  The difference in numbers of individual birds (abundance) was not statistically significant, but the difference in numbers of species was significant during both spring and early summer.

8. Based on abundance and flight elevations, diurnal species most likely to be affected by wind turbines at this study area include Ring-billed Gull, Rock Dove, Red-winged Blackbird, European Starling, Red-tailed Hawk, Canada Goose, American Crow, and Common Grackle.

9. Intensive surveys for bird mortality in the vicinity of the wind turbines yielded only one bird death, which can be confidently, attributed to collision with one of the wind turbines.  This bird (a Red-eyed Vireo) represents a nocturnal spring migrant.

10. An experiment with planted bird carcasses suggests that observers using a standard survey method was able to find only about 40-50% of the small bird carcasses present in the fields near the wind turbines.  Predators remove approximately 26% of the carcasses over a 10 day period.  Even accounting for these factors, however, bird mortality at the two wind turbines was low during this study period.

## **I. Background and Study Objectives**

The inevitable shortage of fossil fuels and environmental effects of carbon dioxide emissions have led to widespread interest in alternative sources of energy generation.  Wind power is a pollution-free alternative that already is contributing to energy supplies in California and elsewhere.  Despite its attractive qualities, wind power is not without environmental impacts. One impact of considerable recent interest is the potential hazard of bird collisions with electricity generating wind turbines.  Collisions with human-made structures are believed to be responsible for the deaths of between 5 and 80 million birds annually (Banks 1979, Avery et al. 1980).  The majority of these deaths occur when birds strike windows of buildings (Klem 1979), but recent studies have shown that wind turbines constructed can also be a major source of fatal collisions, especially for migratory passerines, waterfowl, and diurnal raptors (Winkleman 1985, California Energy Commission 1989, Orloff 1992, Walcott 1995).

Research at Altamont Pass near Livermore, California, concluded that more than 500 raptors (hawks, eagles, and owls) might have died over a two year period as a result of collisions with wind turbines (California Energy Commission 1992).  A separate study by KENETECH Wind power estimated slightly lower but still significant rates of mortality (Curry 1993).

Preliminary investigations of bird mortality risks have been completed recently at several potential wind-energy production sites in the Midwestern U.S.  A study of bird activity at Buffalo Ridge in southwestern Minnesota (Nelson 1993) concluded that most migratory birds fly at elevations well above the height of wind turbines.  The most vulnerable groups of birds at existing designs of wind generation facilities are believed to be raptors and waterfowl (Walcott 1995).  No moralities have been observed by operators at small wind farms in Vermont, New York and Massachusetts, including the largest of these at Princeton, Massachusetts (Jacobs 1993).  Unfortunately, birds killed at these localities are unlikely to have been found by casual observations because of the terrain and vegetation surrounding most of these sites.  According to Jacobs, lack of adequate baseline data poses a problem for wind power developers in the northeastern U.S.

This research is motivated by concerns about bird mortality caused by the operation of

wind generation facilities, together with probability that hundreds of wind turbines eventually will be constructed in eastern Wisconsin and elsewhere in the eastern U.S.

## **II.  Objectives.**

The first part of this study addresses the potential effects of wind power facilities on resident and migratory birds in the vicinity of the Horicon Marsh State Wildlife Area and Horicon National Wildlife Refuge, major centers of bird activity in eastern Wisconsin.  The general approach was to document bird activity levels at progressively greater distances from Horicon Marsh.  Field surveys were carried out during spring migration (March - May), summer breeding season (June - July) and fall migration (September - October) in 1996 and 1997.  The second part of the study collected similar data at a separate site near Shirley, Wisconsin, where two wind turbines were constructed in 1998.  Results from these systematic observations can be used to improve a model of environmental risk assessment for construction and operation of wind power generation structures in Wisconsin.  Finally, we searched intensively for evidence of bird mortality in the vicinity of the two operating wind turbines in order to assess levels of mortality that can be expected mortality during operation of wind generation facilities in Wisconsin.

In summary, the objectives of this work are the following. a) Identify patterns of bird activity in the vicinity of Horicon Marsh and the newly constructed wind power facilities near Shirley, Wisconsin. b) Assess mortality at operating wind power facilities, and c) predict potential effects of the wind generators on migratory and resident birds in eastern Wisconsin.

## **III.  Literature Review.**

Several studies across the United States, most notably in California and Europe, have collected information that might be used to solve the avian-wind interaction problem.  The concern for avian mortality at wind farms dates back to the mid-1970's, when tax incentives led to the first large scale construction of wind farms in the United States.  Some of the first studies were conducted by Judd Howell, at Altamont Wind Pass in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, in California.  The study itself was prompted by a lack of a information concerning the avian

mortality from collisions at wind farms.  It had become evident that some bird species, such as Golden Eagle, were at a greater risk for mortality due to their feeding and roosting habits.  Howell and co-workers determined, “that they (the Golden Eagles) were moving with the wind or sheering across the wind at an acute angle to the rotation of the turbine blades.  Birds would have difficulty seeing the rapidly moving turbine blade along its narrow axis” (Howell 1990).

Initial studies in the Montezuma Hills of Solano County in California were conducted to document the extent of bird activity in the wind tower areas.  These studies focused mainly on raptors and waterfowl, but researchers recorded all avian activity at the study area.  The first two reports from the Montezuma Hills Project (Howell 1998, 1991) involved bird activity at proposed wind turbine locations.  The final report was conducted as a post construction study at the wind energy development site (Howell 1992).

The California Energy Commission started collecting data on bird/wind interactions in November of 1984.  Observers at the Altamont Pass and Tehachapi Pass wind generation facilities documented collisions involving 108 individuals, all of which were raptors.  Ninety percent of the collisions ended in mortality (California Energy Commission 1989).

Wind-avian interactions are being conducted at several other locations in the United States.  Buffalo Ridge, in the southwestern part of Minnesota, is the site of a three-phase wind power plant operated by Northern States Power Company.  The avian study follows a BACI (Before/After and Control/Impact) design, originally proposed by Richard Anderson with the California Energy Commission.  The design combines data collection of avian use prior to construction at the phase II and III sites while it collects data on bird mortality at the post construction phase I site.  The study is mostly concerned with raptors and large waterfowl (Strickland 1998), but recent studies have addresses impacts on grassland birds in the surrounding landscape (Leddy et al. 1999).

Another study in the state of Minnesota employs a radar-based design to determine the probabilities of bird interactions.  Information from different sites is being used to identify the best location (with the lowest risk) for a new wind farm site (Hanowski 1998).  Preliminary results suggest that it is difficult, if not impossible to predict the precise timing and geographic pattern of

bird migration (Hanowski 1998).

A small farm of 11 turbines in Searsburg, VT, is the site of a study headed by the former director of the Cape May Bird Observatory, Paul Kerlinger.  Research at Searsburg is mainly concerned with the breeding and migrating birds of the Green Mountain area (Kerlinger 1998).

The Conservation and Renewable Energy Systems, in Klickitat County, Washington are developing a wind power site.  No turbines currently exist on the site because the original contracted company failed.  However, when construction is finished, approximately 90 turbines will have been erected.  Again, raptors are the primary concern at this site.  This study is using a basic BACI design (Strickland 1998).

SeaWest Energy Corporation is constructing another wind farm in Carbon County, Wyoming.  The associated avian-wind interaction study again follows the BACI design and is headed by Dale Strickland.  This study is not only concerned with raptors and other large birds, but also with the Mountain Plover, a candidate species for state endangered list, which breeds in Wyoming grasslands (Strickland 1998).

Europe has a much longer history in the wind industry than the United States.  However, their wind power farms are all much smaller than those of California.  Because most regions are intensively settled, relatively little area is available for extensive wind energy facilities.

One small wind farm is found in the water off the shore of Netherlands.  Sjored Dirksen is currently studying the effects of these turbines on the daily migrations of scaup and tufted duck. The turbines are potential barriers in the daily flight paths of waterfowl.  One major problem with this study is the fact that the ducks fall into the water and are sometimes lost, therefore, the actual mortality rate is impossible to attain (Dirksen 1998).

Research at another small farm in Tarifa, Spain is mainly concerned with the raptors in the area, including the Griffen Vulture.  This study is headed by Guyonne Janss who found an average mortality rate of 0.34 birds per turbine per year.  Janss and colleagues suggest that wind facilities should  (1) avoid protected sites and (2) be constructed outside protected areas only. Janss et al. also stated that to be completely effective a before construction study should be performed (Janss 1998, Lowther 1998).

Another study in Bryn Titli, Wales is being conducted at a site containing 22 turbines. Researches at Bryn Titli learned that (1) careful/realistic planning of studies is required and (2) account must be taken of all key environmental variables.  Unfortunately pre-construction surveys also were not conducted at this site (Lowther 1998).

Extensive pre-construction data have been collected at the site of 9 wind turbines near Blyth Harbor, Northumbria, and England.  Researchers there demonstrated the importance of long term monitoring and the need to consider many factors in assessing risks of bird mortality (Lowther 1998).

Tuno Knob, another off shore wind farm in Denmark has 10 turbines.  Researchers at this site found that duck numbers in the area were drastically decreasing after construction of the turbines.  However, research suggested that this was probably due to a decrease in food, not necessarily the turbine.  In the end, Lowther and the Tuno Knob researchers recommended that a Europe wide study is needed to gain a clearer understanding of the effects of wind turbines on birds (Lowther 1998).

Several models have been developed to predict the risk of wind turbine collisions on birds. A variety of factors have been employed to determine risk for individual species.  For example, Morrison (1998) used a matrix model encompassing life table information for each species.  He reviewed the major wildlife and ornithological journals to determine patterns of annual survivorship among species.  Morrison determined that passerines are “much more sensitive to changes in the juvenile survival rate than to changes in the adult survival rate.”  Ducks show very little difference in survival rate between the juveniles and adults.  Adult geese are found to be highly sensitive to survival rate changes while the juveniles are not.  Gulls are similar to the geese.  Finally, eagles are similar to gulls only the sensitivity to adult mortality is much more extreme (Morrison 1998).

Erickson (1998) used a relative index model to estimate the risk of impact between birds and wind turbines.  The relative index model is expressed as: I = U*Pf*Pt. where I is the relative index to risk. U is the mean use of species I adjusted for visibility bias. Pf is the proportion of all observations of species I where activity was recorded as flying, and Pt is an index estimating the

percentage of time species I spends flying during the daylight period (Erickson 1998).

More recent papers were presented at a series of conferences called the National AvianWind Power Planning Meetings.  These meetings have been sponsored and attended by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), the American Wind Energy Association, the Electric Power Research Institute, the Department of Energy, the National Audubon Society, the Union of Concerned Scientists and several researchers.  The first of these meetings took place 2021 July, 1994 in Denver, Colorado.  The objectives of this meeting were to (1) identify and prioritize key issues with respect to bird-wind turbine interactions. (2) Define a research agenda to resolve scientific and technical issues, while (3) insuring transferability of results, (4) avoiding duplication and inadequate science, and (5) building consensus on approaches to the research needed to address the issues” (NREL 1994).

Several papers were presented at the 1994 conference, but in the end participants had more questions than answers.  This led to the second meeting of the National Avian-Wind Power Planning in Palm Springs, California on September 20-22, 1995.  By this time, several of the people at the first meeting had formed a committee called the Avian Subcommittee of the National Wind Coordinating Committee, which sponsored this meeting.  Again, research ideas were shared in order to predict and reduce bird mortality from wind turbines.  The purposes of the second meeting were to (1) provide information on avian/wind power interactions that will help meet the needs of regulators, researchers, and other stakeholders concerned with responsible development and permitting of wind plants; (2) create dialogue among regulators, researchers and other stakeholders to help all parties understand the role that research can play in responsible development and permitting of wind plants, and allow researchers to understand the relevance of their research to the process; and (3) propose research projects and the appropriate sponsorship (NREL 1995).

The third meeting in the series took place in San Diego, California on May 27-29, 1998. Several papers and updates of research in the United States and Europe were presented at this meeting, however, the focus was geared toward one of the group’s original goals.  The review draft of the paper, “Studying Wind Energy/Bird Interactions: A Guidance Document.”  was made

available for comments by participants.  The authors of this paper (Richard Anderson with the California Energy Commission, Michael Morrison with California State University, Sacramento, Karin Sinclair with the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and Dale Strickland with Western EcoSystems Technology) outlined how to design and carry out an avian-wind energy interaction study and the proper siting of a new wind energy facility.  This “metrics and methods paper” (as it is called) lay out in a step by step/flow chart format for an ideal study (Anderson et al.1998).

## **IV.  Methods and Study Design. Horicon Study**

This project establishes baseline information for a BACI design.  Our work consists of the “before” part of the design, assuming that at least some towers eventually will be constructed in the Horicon study area.  During 1996, we selected 160 census points along secondary roads at 4 distances from Horicon Marsh: 1 km, 2 km, 4 km and 8 km (shown in Figure 1).  During each visit to the area, a subset of 10 census points was selected randomly by drawing numbers from a hat.  Three points were selected from the 1-km distance, 3 from the 2-km distance 2 from the 4- km distance and 2 from the 8-km distance.  At each point, all birds observed by sight and sound during a 10-minute sampling period were recorded on standardized forms (Appendix A).  The 10minute sampling period was divided into the first 3 minutes, the next 2 minutes and the final 5 minutes to provide compatibility with other avian census projects.  Additional information such as altitude of flight in meters, distance from observer in meters, whether the birds cross an imaginary plane between the observer and the marsh, direction of flight and compass reading of first siting was also gathered.  All of this information was collected by a single observer (Ryan Atwater) to avoid observer differences and biases.  Weather information for each site including wind speed, starting temperature and cloud coverage was collected as well.  Statistical analyses

(e.g. analysis of covariance, with direction from the marsh as a categorical variable and distances

as a covariate) was carried out to examine differences in species diversity, total bird activity, and

abundance of individual species.

Figure 1.  Map of the Horicon Study Area.  Points (solid circles) indicate sampling stations.

Point counts were carried out during spring (March - May), summer (June - July), and Autumn (September - October) during 1996 and 1997.  Although most counts were completed before 10:00 a.m., fieldwork was conducted during all times of day.  Daily surveys included all distances from the marsh, assigned randomly within the available time period.  Fieldwork was not carried on rainy days or when winds exceeded approximately 15 m.p.h.

## **Shirley (Wind Turbine) Study Area**

A similar analysis was carried out in the vicinity of recently constructed wind turbines near Shirley, Wisconsin.  Surveys at this site were conducted during the spring (April-May), early summer (May 25 - June 1), and autumn (September - October) of 1998.  Point counts were conducted at the existing turbine site and at distances of 1 kilometer, 2 km and 4 km from the turbines.  Methods were identical to those employed at the Horicon study area.

The second part of this investigation evaluated bird mortality at the wind tower site west of Shirley.  Searches were conducted in transects following the protocol described by Kimberly Kruse in her avian mortality study at the WAPL radio tower, approximately 300 meters from the wind turbines.  Parallel transects were established 15 meters apart covering the entire field beneath the tower and support wires (Kruse 1995).  Kruse used several of the techniques outlined in Orloff’s studies in the Tehachapi Wind Resource Area.  In our study, 22 transect lines (15 m apart) were sampled in the field surrounding the two turbines.  These transects were walked nearly every day during May 1998 and were sampled at approximately biweekly intervals during autumn 1998, after the surrounding cornfield was harvested.  Field observers included Ryan Atwater, Jeffrey Bell, Kathy Dax, Diane Cooper, Robert Howe, Lori Johansen, Jerad Linneman, Todd McCoy, and John Reisenbuechler.  Any evidence of bird strikes such as feathers and carcasses were collected and identified with the help of Thomas Erdman, Curator of the Richter Museum at UWGB.  Data again were recorded on standardized forms (Appendix B).

During fall 1998, a controlled study was carried out to determine the rate of scavenging on the dead birds and the efficiency of the collectors in finding carcasses.  Birds of various sizes were randomly placed in the field near the turbines and the observers surveyed the field using the

same methods applied during the 1998 migration periods.  Locations of the “planted” carcasses were checked regularly to evaluate rates of removal by animal scavengers.

Eventually, we will attempt to develop a computer program to simulate the probability of birds encountering the proposed and existing wind power structures.  Based on field results, this analysis will identify the probability of birds passing points in “air space” at different elevations and at different potential wind power sites.

Comparisons of bird activity levels at progressively greater distances from Horicon Marsh will help guide decisions aimed at minimizing bird mortality.  The two-year analysis provides some indication of year-to-year variation in bird numbers.  Dependent variables associated with each bird census locality include total numbers of birds, total number of birds in selected ecological guilds or species, and scores from multivariate principal components analysis of all species.  Results can be used to improve a model of environmental risk assessment for construction and operation of the wind power generation structures.

Standard English names of birds follow the American Ornithologists’ Union (1998) Checklist of North American Birds, Seventh Edition (scientific names are not included here).  All statistical tests were carried out with SAS for Windows Version 6.12 (SAS Institute).

## **V. Results**

## **Horicon Bird Surveys**

Sites at the Horicon study area were established during March 1996 and were visited on 84 dates (49 in 1996, 37 in 1997).  Altogether 1030 point samples were completed (Table 1).  We recorded 98 species during the 2-year investigation.  During all seasons, counts were dominated by a few common species (Figure 2, Table 2).  Red-winged Blackbird and European Starling were among the three most abundant species in all seasons, while the Canada Goose was most abundant during all but summer counts.

The order of species depends on whether total abundance or frequency is considered.   Notably, species like Ring-billed Gull and Lapland Longspur were observed relatively infrequently, but large flocks inflated total numbers.  During autumn, for example, Ring-billed Gulls were the third most abundant species, but they were only the 20[th] most frequently observed).  During spring Lapland Longspurs were the 4[th] most abundant species, but the 36[th] most frequently observed. Notable species recorded during this investigation included Merlin (observed twice), Northern Harrier, Cooper’s Hawk, Sharp-shinned Hawk, Great Egret, and Western Meadowlark.

Differences in total numbers of birds or numbers of species were not statistically significant between years (ANOVA, p > .05), so we pooled results in the subsequent analyses. Both the total numbers of individuals and the numbers of species were affected by distance from Horicon Marsh, but not during all seasons.  Numbers of individuals in the vicinity of the marsh were higher during spring and significantly higher during autumn (Figure 3).  During summer, numbers of birds were lower overall, and no distance effect was evident.  Numbers of species were higher near the marsh during spring and summer, with no significant difference during autumn (Figure 4).

Figure 2.  Relative abundance (total count) and frequency of birds at the Horicon study area during 1996 and 1997.

As expected, the numbers of birds were highest during the spring and autumn migration

periods.  Interestingly, however, the mean numbers of species at all distances were lowest during autumn (Figure 4).  This occurs because the autumn migration period seems to cover a longer period, and some of the summer residents depart the area by late summer or early autumn.  Large numbers of individuals in autumn are influenced greatly by flocks of Canada Geese and Redwinged Blackbirds (Table 2).

A significant difference in numbers of birds was related to direction from the center of Horicon Marsh (Figure 5).  During both spring and autumn migration periods, significantly more birds were recorded in the western and northwestern portions of the study area.  Explanations for this directional pattern will be the subject of a more detailed vegetation analysis, and may be related to habitat conditions within the marsh itself.

Elevation of birds above the ground was highly variable (Figure 6), but highest, on average, during autumn.  Many flocks of Canada Geese (Figure 7), Mallards, and Sandhill Cranes were observed at elevations of 50 m or higher.  Species with average elevations greater than 30 m included Double-crested Cormorant, Rough-legged Hawk, Turkey Vulture, and Ring-billed Gull, in addition to Mallard and Sandhill Crane.

Many of the birds recorded during the point surveys occurred at or near the ground, and rarely flew at elevations high enough to be at risk from wind turbines.  In order to provide a more meaningful analysis of species that are likely to be affected by wind turbine construction, we calculated the overall number of occurrences (flocks or solitary individuals) of birds flying at 30m elevation or higher (Table 3).  Like previous studies, this analysis emphasizes the risk of raptors (e.g., Red-tailed Hawk) and water birds (Canada Goose, Mallard).

## **Shirley (Wind Turbine) Bird Surveys**

Like Horicon, the Shirley study area is inhabited and visited by birds typical of agricultural landscapes in eastern Wisconsin (as shown in Table 4).  During the more limited field surveys, we recorded 70 species (compared with 98 at the Horicon study area).  Red-winged Blackbird was prominent during all three seasons (spring, early summer, autumn), along with Killdeer, Savanna Sparrow, American Robin, and European Starling (Table 3).  Some important seasonal differences were observed.  Rock Doves, presumably in response to waste grain in farm fields and cessation of nesting, became increasingly abundant towards autumn.  Ring-billed Gulls were abundant during spring and early summer, but were relatively infrequent during autumn. Likewise, Horned Lark, Savanna Sparrow, and Western Meadowlark were appreciably less common in autumn.  Notable species that were more abundant during autumn included American Pipit, Lapland Longspur, Red-tailed Hawk, and Black-bellied Plover.

The distribution of birds with respect to the wind turbines showed that fewer birds (Figure 8) and fewer species (Figure 9) were recorded in the vicinity of the turbines.  The differences were statistically significant (p < .05, ANOVA) for number of species but for total bird numbers.

## **Avian Mortality Study**

Intensive surveys of bird mortality at the Shirley wind turbines were carried out during the spring and autumn migration periods of 1998 using the systematic method described above. Each transects survey typically required between 2 to 3 hours.  We completed a total of 54 surveys during March (3), April (4), May (11), September (6), October (20), November (8), December (2), 1998.  During this time, only a single bird, a Red-eyed Vireo collected on May 22[nd] , approximately 40 m from one of the wind turbines, appears to have clearly been killed by operation of the wind turbines.  (Both turbines were operating when the bird was discovered.) Another complete carcass of a Yellow-rumped Warbler was collected on September 27[th] on the road north of the wind generators, but this bird likely was killed by one of the radio towers north of the road.  On October 13[th] , feathers and fresh blood from a Killdeer, but no carcass, were identified and photographed approximately 60 m east of the southern wind turbine.  This bird might have been killed by the wind turbine and removed by a scavenger, but the remains also

might represent a kill by a predator.  During 1998 we observed a House Cat, Raccoon (tracks), Red-tailed Hawk, Peregrine, and Northern Harrier in the vicinity of the wind turbines.

Feather remains were documented on 9 other occasions, in all cases consisting of a few isolated feathers that might have been lost from molting birds or from an unsuccessful predator attack.  These feathers belonged to another Killdeer (May 11[th] ), a Mourning Dove (September 27), a Rock Dove (May 23[rd] , October 30[th] ) and unknown species, probably Rock Doves.

On 15 October 49 carcasses of Ovenbirds were placed within the area visited by the field observers.  Approximately half of these (25 birds) were distributed randomly, stratified by linear transect (Appendix B), while the other half (24 birds) were systematically placed in perpendicular lines in order to insure that they could be found later.  Additional 50 carcasses representing a variety of species were placed in two lines on November 8[th] .  Many of the first set of birds were lost when the eastern half of the field was plowed on approximately November 1.  Recovery rates have been adjusted to account for the destroyed carcasses.

Conditions in the field during October were excellent for relocating the carcasses; little vegetation was present, and the dark soil had been plowed within the previous month. Nevertheless, these small bird carcasses proved to be difficult to find, even for the observers who had placed the randomly distributed birds in the first place.  If we exclude the birds placed in perpendicular lines, only 58% of the birds placed in the field could be relocated by the same observers (with directions from a crude map) two days later.  Field observers who did not have directions to the carcass localities fared even poorer, finding approximately 40 - 50% of the carcasses (Figure 11).  Hence, we can assume that a significant amount of tower killed birds will be overlooked by our sampling method.

As days passed from the initial placement of the birds, recovery rates declined as scavengers removed some of the birds (Figure 11).  An estimate of this removal rate can be obtained by following the fate of the linear-placed birds which were easily relocated (Figure 12). The regression line describing the removal of birds follows the formula: Y = 1.0 - 0.026X, where Y is the proportion of the original birds still at the site, and X is the number of days since the birds were first present in the field (r[2] = 0.967, p < .001, standard regression analysis).  This

analysis provides the rule of thumb that approximately 25% of the birds will be removed after 10 days.

## **VI. Discussion**

Risks of bird collisions at wind turbines are a function of two factors: 1) presence of birds at an appropriate elevation in the vicinity of the turbine and, and 2) behavior of the birds causing avoidance of or attraction to the turbines.  This study mainly addresses the first of these factors. We have identified the most abundant species at in the vicinity of Horicon Marsh, where wind power facilities are being considered, and at the existing wind turbines near Shirley, Wisconsin. Species composition at the two sites differed, clearly reflecting differences in land use and nearby bird habitats.  Based on local abundance, the highest risks of collisions in the vicinity of Horicon Marsh exist for large water birds (Canada Goose, Mallard, Sandhill Crane) and raptors or scavengers (red-tailed Hawk, American Crow, Ring-billed Gull, Turkey Vulture).  At the Shirley site, birds of agricultural habitats (Rock Dove, Red-winged Blackbird, European Starling, Common Grackle), in addition to Ring-billed Gull, Red-tailed Hawk, and Canada Goose) are the most likely candidates (among diurnal birds) for collisions.  Our analysis does not address the diversity and abundance of nocturnal bird species, which should be evaluated before a complete risk assessment of bird collisions, is attempted.

Horicon Marsh clearly attracts thousands of birds as both breeders and migratory visitors. Not surprisingly, numbers of birds in the surrounding fields and airspace are higher near the marsh than at increasing distances from the marsh.  Our results show that spatial patterns of birds in the vicinity of Horicon Marsh are complex and seasonal, however.  Birds tend to be concentrated near the Marsh more in autumn and, to a lesser extent, during spring.  The northwestern and western directions are used most frequently by birds than other directions, again, especially during migration periods.  These results suggest that bird activity is much reduced at distances of 8 km from the edge of the Horicon Marsh.  Construction of wind generators at distances 8 km or greater will have significantly lower impacts than generators closer to the marsh.

Results from the Shirley site also show a geographic pattern of bird distribution and abundance.  In this case, the number of bird species (and to a lesser extent number of individual

birds) increases as we go away from the existing wind turbines.  This is similar to recent findings of Leddy et al. (1999), who found that densities of grassland birds in Minnesota were lower in the vicinity of wind turbines than in similar habitats 180 m or more from the turbines.  Our results are complicated by the fact that, except for a small wood lot near the radio towers, the habitat near the turbines is open and intensively farmed.  At least some of the sites at 1, 2, and 4 km from the turbines included more extensive forest and wetland habitats.  The presence of three large radio transmission towers (Kruse 1995) within 300 m of the wind turbines also might have had an additional effect on bird diversity and abundance.

Despite the lower numbers of species near the wind turbines, both numbers of species and numbers of individuals at the Shirley study area (Figures 8 and 9) were higher than at the Horicon study area (Figures 3 and 4).  This unexpected difference was not due to differences in the timing of our samples, because similar results are obtained if we compare the data over exactly the same time period (May and September/October).  Several factors might be responsible for the observed difference, including greater visibility, a greater diversity of habitats (a small woodland was present even near the wind turbines), and of course, genuinely greater numbers of birds at the Shirley study area.  Additional analysis will be required to explain this finding.

Risks of bird mortality at wind power facilities clearly vary seasonally.  During autumn, more individual birds (many of them young and inexperienced) are present at both the Horicon and Shirley study areas.  Furthermore, the average elevation of diurnal birds is higher (Figures 6 and 10) during autumn, leading to greater potential for collision.  In both areas, summer appears to be the time when collision risks are lowest, assuming that behavior of birds does not vary appreciably with respect to vulnerability of collisions.

Intensive searches for bird carcasses in the vicinity of the wind turbines yielded only a single case of probable turbine-related mortality.  The species (Red-eyed Vireo) is not resident in the immediate area, and this bird probably was a nocturnal migrant.  Other studies in the eastern U.S. (Jacobs 1993) have failed to show any mortality at wind turbines, and our findings are consistent with the notion that fatal collisions are relatively rare.  Bird collisions with towers, on

the other hand, are notoriously episodic (Kemper 1964, Walcott 1995), and additional studies will be needed in order to conclude that wind turbines pose little or no threat to birds.

Our experiment study at the Shirley site demonstrated that observers were unable to find a significant number of carcasses that were known to be present.  Although significant scatter exists, the data suggest that under conditions that existed during autumn 1999 (plowed field) and the method used by our field observers. Only about 40% of small bird carcasses are likely to be discovered immediately after the collision (Figure 11).  And, predators and scavengers at the rate of about 25% subsequently remove the carcasses over 10 days (Figure 12).  These results are consistent with the results reported by Kruse (1995), that estimated a sampling efficiency (using the same method as ours) between 33-50%.  Even accounting for a substantial error in bird discovery, the total numbers of moralities at the Shirley wind turbines appears to have been small, probably less than 10 birds during spring and fall migration periods of 1998.

The potential effects of wind turbines on birds are a very active area of research, leading to a growing literature of articles and reports (Leddy et al. 1999, Nelson and Curry 1995, Sommerhage 1994, Ivanov 1993, Orloff and Flannery 1992).  Results from our investigation add another piece of evidence to the collective knowledge about the effects of wind power development on birds, and provide baseline information for comparisons with future studies at the Horicon and Shirley study areas.  Additional analysis will be incorporated into the Master’s thesis of Ryan Atwater, which will address the effects of habitat characteristics and other factors on bird distribution patterns in these study areas.
